title: Workflow Analysis
summary: Workflow analysis compares intended workflows with actual work as performed. It produces role-specific workflow maps, workaround catalogues, error catalogues, handoff analysis and inputs for microtask analysis and task-criticality mapping.
keyFacts: Workflow analysis maps actual workflows rather than intended workflows.
The practice is primarily used during Sandbox Experiments before design decisions are made.
In multi-role systems, workflow analysis is conducted per role rather than aggregated across roles.
The practice requires observation, not only interview, because complex professional work includes tacit sequences and rapid decisions that practitioners cannot fully reconstruct retrospectively.
Methods include in-situ observation, contextual interview, protocol walkthroughs, documentation analysis and session recording analysis.

Session recording analysis can substitute for or supplement direct observation when direct observation is not feasible, but it does not capture contextual conditions, time pressures or external factors around interface use.
Outputs include role-specific workflow maps, workaround catalogues, error catalogues, handoff-point identification and inputs for microtask analysis and task-criticality mapping.
Triopsis evidence included 3 in-situ observation sessions under operational pressure and drove a 47-microtask analysis.
IDEXX Animana evidence included workflow analysis across 35 clinics, 3 countries and 4 role types over 2 weeks.
Enhesa evidence included 95 session recordings, 31 documented workarounds across 4 categories and 12 error types with time-to-redress measurement.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies workflow analysis as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Documents Actual Work Rather Than Intended Process
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis is the practice of documenting the actual operational sequences through which work gets done, including deviations, workarounds, informal adaptations and handoffs that are absent from process documentation or user self-report.

The central distinction in workflow analysis is between designed workflow and actual workflow. A workflow diagram drawn from requirements or stakeholder interviews describes how the system was intended to operate. Workflow analysis describes how practitioners complete work under real conditions.

In complex professional systems, the gap between intended workflow and actual workflow is often the main finding. The practice records real sequences, decision points, deviations, role-spanning handoffs and workarounds that may not appear in requirements, process documents or retrospective accounts.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Treats Divergence From The Designed Process As Evidence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis produces a role-specific map of actual work. It shows where the system supports the work, where the system resists the work, which informal practices have developed to compensate for interface failures and which informal practices preserve operational knowledge that a redesign should not remove.

A parallel spreadsheet, a printed reference sheet, a checklist taped to a monitor or a repeated navigation pattern can indicate that the interface does not support the work as performed. The same artefact can also contain useful operational knowledge that needs to survive redesign.

In multi-role systems, workflow analysis is conducted per role. A scheduler's workflow, a field technician's workflow and an operations manager's workflow are distinct. Aggregating role workflows can produce a composite account that is accurate for none of the roles.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Is Used Before Design Decisions And During System Audits
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis is primarily used during Sandbox Experiments before design decisions are made. In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, Sandbox Experiments are used to understand the operational reality of the system before committing to interface structure, workflow architecture or detailed interaction behaviour.

Workflow analysis is also used diagnostically in audits of existing systems. In that setting, the purpose is to understand what the platform supports and does not support before recommending changes.

Direct observation is preferred when the operational context permits it. In-situ observation can reveal tacit sequences, informal adaptations and rapid decisions that practitioners may not reconstruct accurately in retrospective interviews.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Combines Observation, Walkthroughs, Documentation Review And Recordings
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis uses observation and supporting research methods in combination. Interview evidence alone is insufficient for complex professional work because practitioners may not be able to describe tacit routines, rapid judgements or adaptations made under pressure.

In-situ observation records work in the actual operational environment under real conditions. Contextual interview asks practitioners to describe work while doing it or immediately after completing a task. Protocol walkthroughs ask practitioners to describe specific workflows as if teaching them to a newcomer.

Documentation analysis reviews existing process documents, training materials and system specifications to establish the intended workflow. The gap between intended workflow and actual workflow becomes the starting point for investigation.

Session recording analysis systematically reviews recorded usage sessions from a deployed platform to reconstruct actual user behaviour at scale. In-situ observation provides contextual depth; session recording analysis provides behavioural breadth. The two methods are complementary when both are available.

bodySections.heading: Session Recording Analysis Has Behavioural Breadth But Limited Context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Session recording analysis can substitute for or supplement in-situ observation when direct observation is not feasible. This situation can occur when a platform is already deployed at scale, when the user base is geographically distributed or when the operational context does not permit in-person access.

Session recordings capture what users do with the interface, but not the contextual conditions, time pressures or external factors that caused those behaviours. Session recording analysis is most appropriate when the platform generates sufficient session data and when workaround patterns are visible in interface interactions.

Visible patterns can include navigation errors, repeated attempts and unexpected path choices. Patterns that depend on physical or organisational context may not be visible in recordings.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Outputs Role Maps, Workaround Catalogues And Error Catalogues
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis produces a documented map of actual workflows per role. The map records sequences, decision points and deviations from the designed flow.

Workflow analysis produces a catalogue of workaround patterns. Each workaround is tagged as either a failure signal, where the system is not supporting what users need to do, or a preservation signal, where the workaround encodes operational knowledge that should be carried forward.

Workflow analysis produces a catalogue of error types. The catalogue identifies recurring failure conditions across the user population, with frequency and, where measurable, the time cost of detection and recovery. Error catalogues inform both error prevention design and error recovery design.

Workflow analysis identifies handoff points where work or context passes between roles. These handoff points are primary failure locations in multi-role systems.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Provides Inputs For Microtask Analysis And Task-Criticality Mapping
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis provides the empirical starting point for microtask analysis and task-criticality mapping. Workflow analysis identifies the boundaries of significant workflows; microtask analysis decomposes them into discrete actions, and task-criticality mapping assesses which tasks carry the highest operational consequence.

The research protocol for workflow analysis can change as early sessions reveal patterns. If a workaround appears in the first clinic, workshop or observation session, later sessions can probe that pattern explicitly. Workflow analysis in complex operational contexts does not depend on a fixed protocol when emerging evidence changes what needs to be investigated.

bodySections.heading: Workflow Analysis Evidence Must Distinguish Observation, Recordings, Client Material And Design Reasoning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflow analysis should not treat every workflow artefact as field observation. Observed operational work, session recording analysis, client-stated accounts, document-derived flows and design reasoning from operating conditions have different evidential status.

Observed work can support claims about actual behaviour under specific conditions. Session recordings can support claims about interface behaviour at scale, but have limited contextual evidence. Client-stated accounts and document-derived flows can describe understood or intended work, but should not be treated as Creative Navy observation. Design reasoning from operating conditions can explain a design split or workflow structure, but should not be presented as a researched workflow finding.

strongClaims: Workflow analysis documents actual operational sequences, deviations, workarounds, informal adaptations and handoffs rather than intended workflow diagrams.
Workflow analysis is primarily used during Sandbox Experiments before design decisions and diagnostically during audits of existing systems.
In multi-role systems, workflow analysis must be conducted per role rather than aggregated across roles.

Workflow analysis requires observation, not only interview, because complex professional work includes tacit sequences, informal adaptations and rapid decisions that practitioners cannot fully reconstruct retrospectively.

Session recording analysis can substitute for or supplement in-situ observation when direct observation is not feasible, but it lacks contextual evidence about conditions, time pressure and external factors.
Triopsis workflow analysis involved 3 in-situ observation sessions under operational pressure and drove a 47-microtask analysis and redesign of the exception-handling architecture.
IDEXX Animana workflow analysis covered 35 clinics, 3 countries, 2 weeks and 4 role types, and found incompatible cognitive requirements between reception and clinical roles.

Enhesa workflow research used 95 session recordings, documented 31 workarounds across four categories, documented 12 error types with time-to-redress measurement and addressed 80% of documented workarounds in the redesign.
Assemblio and Oceaneering workflow material should not be treated as in-situ observation evidence.
limitations: Session recordings capture interface behaviour but not the contextual conditions, time pressures or external factors that caused that behaviour.
Workflow analysis should be role-specific in multi-role systems; aggregated cross-role maps may misrepresent each role's actual work.
Assemblio workflow material was built from client material and client-stated accounts, not Creative Navy observation.
Oceaneering workflow material surfaced during review rather than in requirements or observed dispatch operations; no dispatch operator was observed and no depot was visited.
AIT workflow splitting was design reasoning from physical operating conditions, not a researched workflow finding, and the engagement involved no user research.
The industrial automation engagement describes designed responses for a product in development and should not be read as an outcome claim.
No engagement dates are stated; the evidence uses sequence, duration and counts only where documented.
